clips.title: I Told My AI Agent Not to Use the Key. It Did, 8 of 20 Times
clips.why: A small, honest experiment: an agent could read a decoy key and was told not to use it, and the title already gives the result, 8 times out of 20 it used the key anyway.
look: Watch how the decoy test is set up: a key the agent can read, and a rule in the prompt telling it not to use it.
Notice that the rule is a request. It lowers the number, but it does not make it zero.
Ask yourself what the agent could do if the key were not on the machine at all.
clips.after: Our harness takes the same lesson further: the VM holds no Anthropic key at all, only a run token that works through our gateway for one run.

clips.title: I Told My AI Agent Not to Use the Key. It Did, 8 of 20 Times
clips.why: The second test runs a public set of attack prompts against the agent, to see how much a rule in the prompt really protects.
look: Watch whether the rule stops the attacks, or only some of them.
Listen for the conclusion in the chapter title: rules help, but lower is not zero.
Think about what would stop the rest: a check in code that runs before every tool call.
clips.after: A check in code that runs before every tool call is exactly what our PreToolUse hooks are: blockWalls checks every Edit and Bash call before it runs, whatever the prompt says.

clips.title: Hooks in Claude Code
clips.why: Anthropic's own short tour of hooks: code that runs at fixed moments, such as before a tool is used or after a file is edited.
look: Blocking a dangerous operation before it happens: that is our PreToolUse wall.
Formatting a file right after an edit: that is our PostToolUse lint hook.
Hooks are shared with the team through settings. The harness loads fcp's project settings, so fcp's own hooks also run inside Nova's session.
clips.after: Nova's harness registers the same kinds of hooks in code, with one addition you will not see here: every refusal also goes into the refusal ledger for the PR.

clips.title: LiteLLM: Free Open Source Gateway to Manage All Your LLM Providers
clips.why: A gateway hands out its own keys that are not the provider's key, which is the idea behind our run token.
look: Notice that the provider's real key stays inside the gateway.
Watch how each virtual key is created on its own, so it can be tracked and limited on its own.
Ask yourself what happens to the real key when one virtual key is removed.
clips.after: Our gateway is our own service, not LiteLLM, but the run token plays the role of a virtual key that lives for one run only.

practice.q: The env option replaces the whole subprocess environment. Finish the first line so Bash still has PATH and HOME.
practice.hint: Spread the parent process's environment first.
practice.why: Without the spread the session gets only the two gateway variables, so tools lose PATH, HOME and the image's proxy settings. Our values come after, so they win.

practice.q: Which value goes into ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN on a sandbox VM?

options.text: The team's Anthropic API key, read from Vault at start
options.why: Vault is never reachable from the VM, and a key in the VM is exactly what the design avoids.

options.text: The run token the orchestrator minted for this run
options.why: The gateway checks it, adds the real key and counts the cost. It dies when the run ends.

options.text: Nothing; the gateway knows which VM is calling
options.why: The gateway needs the token to know which run is calling, so it can refuse strangers and tag the cost.

practice.q: The model tries Edit on .github/workflows/frontend-ci.yml. What should the hook return?

options.text: {} so the normal permission rules decide
options.why: Edit is in allowedTools, so the rules would allow it. The wall must decide.
A bare no invites the model to try the same thing another way. Give it a reason and an alternative.

options.text: A deny with a reason and an alternative, recorded in the refusal ledger
options.why: The model reads the reason as the tool's answer and changes course, and the ledger shows the reviewer what was tried.

practice.q: Complete the hook's matcher so the CI wall sees every tool that writes a file.
practice.hint: Three built-in tools write files: one edits, one writes a whole file, one edits notebooks.
practice.why: The matcher decides which calls reach the hook. Leave out Write and the model can replace the whole workflow file instead of editing it.

practice.q: Put what happens when the VM freezes in order, from the transcript's point of view.
items: Each batch of transcript entries is uploaded to the run's folder through a presigned URL
The VM freezes and the workflow claims a fresh VM
The fresh VM's harness starts a session with resume and the old session id
The SDK calls load, which reads the parts in name order
The model continues with everything it read and was told before
practice.why: The store is written as the session goes, so the conversation is already outside the VM when the machine dies.

practice.q: On the VM, the model calls a tool that is not in allowedTools, and the hook returns {}. permissionMode is "dontAsk". What happens?

options.text: The call is refused at once, and the model reads the refusal as the tool's answer
options.why: {} means the hook has no opinion, so the normal rules decide, and dontAsk refuses anything that is not allowed instead of asking.

options.text: The session waits until a person approves the call
options.why: That is what the default mode does, and nobody sits at a prompt on the VM, so the run would wait forever. That is why we set dontAsk.

options.text: The call runs, because the hook did not deny it
options.why: An empty answer from a hook is not an approval. It hands the decision to the normal permission rules.
